paragraphs.heading: What a bond is
paragraphs.text: A chemical bond is an attraction between atoms. It is what lets atoms or ions join up into molecules, crystals and other structures. Bonds hold together the atoms of molecules, crystals, metals and other forms of matter, and the bonds decide how the material is built and how it behaves. The differences between kinds of bond come from how the outermost electrons of the atoms, called valence electrons, behave.

paragraphs.heading: Strong and weak bonds
paragraphs.text: A bond can come from the pull between ions of opposite charge, which makes an ionic bond, from atoms sharing electrons, which makes a covalent bond, or from a mix of both. Chemists also sort bonds by strength. Covalent, ionic and metallic bonds count as strong or primary bonds. Hydrogen bonds, the London dispersion force and dipole–dipole interactions count as weak or secondary ones. The kinds shade into each other with no clear border, yet naming them separately is still useful, since they give materials different properties.

paragraphs.heading: Why atoms stick together
paragraphs.text: Opposite charges attract, so the negative electrons around an atom and the positive protons in its nucleus pull on each other. An electron shared by two nuclei is pulled by both of them. Bonded nuclei settle at a best spacing, the bond distance, where attraction and repulsion balance. Forming a bond releases energy. This is not because potential energy drops, since the extra attractions are offset by repulsions; it comes from a fall in the electrons' kinetic energy when they spread over a larger region instead of staying close to one nucleus.

paragraphs.heading: Covalent bonds
paragraphs.text: Picture a covalent bond at its simplest: one or more electrons, often a pair, are drawn into the space between two nuclei. Such a bond joins two particular atoms and points in a set direction, which is why drawings show it as a line and models show it as a stick between balls. When the electrons are shared unequally, the bond is called polar. Covalent bonds often build small, well-connected groups of atoms called molecules. In solids and liquids these molecules hold onto each other only through much weaker forces, which is why waxes and oils are soft and melt at low temperatures.

paragraphs.heading: Chains and networks
paragraphs.text: Covalent bonds can also link atoms into long chains, as in nylon, or run as networks through a whole solid, as in diamond and quartz. The result can then be both strong and tough. Such polymers and networks also melt at much higher temperatures.

paragraphs.heading: Ionic bonds
paragraphs.text: In a simple picture of an ionic bond, an electron is handed over rather than shared. One nucleus offers the electron a more tightly held place than the other, so one atom can pass an electron to its neighbour. That leaves one atom with a net positive charge and the other with a net negative charge, and the two charged particles, called ions, attract each other. Ionic bonds are strong, so these substances need high temperatures to melt, but they are brittle because the forces between ions reach only a short way. Crystals of table salt get their character from this kind of bond.

paragraphs.heading: Metallic bonds
paragraphs.text: In a metal, each atom gives one or more electrons to a shared sea of electrons lying among many atoms. Each of these electrons can be linked with a great many atoms at once. The atoms, left somewhat positive, stay bound because the loose electrons are attracted to all of them. This bonding is often very strong, which gives metals their tensile strength, yet the atoms are not held in fixed directions, so metal crystals deform more easily and metals are malleable. The same electron cloud explains why metals conduct electricity and heat well and look shiny.
